title: Improvising with Pentatonics
description: Start making up your own melodies with the C major pentatonic, where it's very hard to hit a wrong note.

steps.title: A safe place to start
steps.description: The C major pentatonic has five notes: C, D, E, G, A. No two of them are a half step apart, so nothing clashes. That makes it a great playground for improvising. Whatever order you play them in, it holds together.

steps.title: Play the scale
steps.description: Play up through the five notes: C, D, E, G, A. Get a feel for where they sit under your hand.
steps.hint: Take a C major scale and leave out F and B. Any octave works.

steps.title: Repeat yourself
steps.description: Random notes rarely sound like a tune. Repetition is what makes a melody. Pick three or four notes (a motif), play them, then play them again with a small change. Your ear hears that as an idea instead of a jumble.

steps.title: Try a motif
steps.description: Play E, G, A, one after another. It's a simple three-note idea to build on.
steps.hint: Start on the E just above middle C, then G, then A.

steps.title: Play with rhythm
steps.description: You can get lots of different melodies out of just two or three notes by changing the rhythm. Make some notes short and quick, and let others ring. Don't be afraid of silence, either. A pause between phrases gives the listener a moment to take it in.

steps.title: Low, then high
steps.description: Now stretch out. Play low C (C3), then jump up to A4. Big leaps like this make a melody feel wider and more exciting.
steps.hint: C3 is the C an octave below middle C. A4 is just above middle C, past G. Play them one after the other.

steps.title: The call
steps.description: Musicians often trade phrases like a conversation: one phrase asks, the next one answers. Play the call: E, G, A, at a steady pace.
steps.hint: Same three notes as your first motif. Leave a little pause after the A.

steps.title: The response
steps.description: Now answer it with D, E, G. Similar shape, a little lower, so it sounds like a reply.
steps.hint: Keep the same rhythm as your call. The small change in notes is what makes it feel like an answer.

steps.title: Spot the pentatonic
steps.description: Which of these sets uses only notes from C major pentatonic?

steps.title: Your turn
steps.description:
Now just play. Use C, D, E, G and A in any octave, and try:

• Repeating a short motif
• Changing up the rhythm
• Leaving space between phrases
• Playing some notes soft and others loud

There really aren't any wrong notes here, so experiment.
